A taller than normal back-wall echo plus an extra echo from the lamination
No change at all to the usual single back-wall echo seen on screen
A widening of the main bang spike at the far left of the sweep
content.explanation: The lamination reflects sound early, raising an intermediate echo at its own depth (often near mid-wall in rolled plate, but wherever the lamination lies) and stealing energy from the back wall.
distractors: Laminations reduce, not increase, the back wall.
A lamination changes the display.
The main bang is not where a lamination appears.

content.stem: The back-reflection (loss of back wall) technique detects flaws by:
options: Noting a drop in back-wall amplitude when sound is intercepted by a flaw
Reading the refracted wedge angle off the scale each time the flaw is crossed
Watching the couplant temperature climb the moment the beam meets a flaw
Measuring the height of the main bang spike at the start of the sweep
content.explanation: A flaw that blocks or scatters the beam reduces the back-wall echo, signaling its presence.
distractors: The back-reflection technique watches back-wall amplitude, not wedge angle.
Couplant temperature is not the method.
The main bang is not the back-reflection indicator.

content.stem: The multiple-back-reflection method is useful for:
options: Assessing attenuation and detecting conditions that damp the echo train
Setting the refracted angle of the beam before scanning a weld body
Generating surface waves that skim across the top of the plate
Setting the reference sensitivity from the first back-wall echo height
content.explanation: Comparing the decay of successive back-wall echoes reveals attenuation and scattering conditions in the material.
distractors: It has nothing to do with refracted angle.
It does not create surface waves.
The method assesses attenuation from the echo train, not sensitivity setup.

content.stem: Straight-beam thickness gauging measures thickness from:
options: The time of flight to the back wall and back
The refracted angle read off the block scale
The amount of couplant under the moving probe
The reject level set to clear the baseline
content.explanation: Thickness equals velocity times the round-trip time divided by two.
distractors: Thickness gauging uses time, not angle.
Couplant is not the measurement basis.
Reject does not measure thickness; time of flight does.

content.stem: Welds are commonly inspected with angle-beam probes because:
options: Weld flaws are often not parallel to the surface and the crown blocks straight-beam access
Angle-beam scanning simply covers the entire weld much faster than any straight beam can
Straight beams cannot pass through carbon steel weld metal at all in order to reach flaws
Angle-beam probes work fully dry and need no couplant at all on the weld surface
content.explanation: Angle beams reach the fusion faces and root at favorable angles and scan from beside the reinforcement.
distractors: Speed is not the reason.
Straight beams work in steel.
Angle beams still require couplant.

content.stem: The first leg of an angle-beam path covers:
options: From the entry surface down to the back wall
From the back wall up to the scanning surface
Only the weld crown nearest the entry side
Through the immersion water path to the part
content.explanation: The first leg runs from the scanning surface down to the far surface of the part.
distractors: That is the second leg.
The first leg covers the lower portion, not just the crown.
There is no water path in contact angle-beam testing.

content.stem: The second leg of an angle-beam path covers:
options: From the back wall back up to the scanning surface
From the entry surface straight down to the back wall
Through the wedge before the beam enters the part
Across the couplant film right at the entry surface
content.explanation: After reflecting off the back wall, the second leg returns the beam up toward the scanning surface.
distractors: That is the first leg.
The wedge is before the legs begin.
Couplant is not a leg of the path.

content.stem: Half-skip distance corresponds to the beam reaching:
options: The back wall (one leg)
The surface (two legs)
Past the surface again
Only the weld crown
content.explanation: At half skip the beam has traveled one leg to the back wall; a full skip returns it to the surface.
distractors: That is full skip.
That exceeds a full skip.
Half skip is defined by the back wall, not the crown.

content.stem: To cover the full weld volume, the operator typically:
options: Moves the probe toward and away from the weld while traversing its length
Holds the probe fixed at a single spot beside the weld for the entire scan
Scans only the upper half of the weld thickness from a single side
Uses just one leg at one fixed standoff for the entire weld length
content.explanation: A raster or zigzag motion (forward-and-back plus along the weld) sweeps the beam through the entire weld cross-section.
distractors: A stationary probe misses most of the volume.
The full thickness must be covered.
Both legs and a range of positions are needed.

content.stem: Rotating or orbiting the probe around an indication helps to:
options: Characterize the reflector and maximize its signal
Shorten the sound path running back to the probe
Push the reflector clear of the dead zone
Apply a transfer correction to the reading itself
content.explanation: Orbital and rotational moves peak the echo and help judge the reflector's shape and orientation.
distractors: Rotation peaks the echo; it does not shorten the path.
Rotation characterizes the reflector; it does not change the dead zone.
Rotation is not transfer correction.

content.stem: The standard angle-beam weld scan, with the beam directed across the weld axis, is oriented to detect:
options: Cracks running along the length of the weld (longitudinal cracks)
Laminations lying flat within the adjacent base-metal plate body
The surface roughness of the cap running along the weld crown
Whether the couplant is wetting the weld surface evenly
content.explanation: Directing the beam across the weld puts it near-perpendicular to the faces of longitudinally oriented cracks, so the standard scan detects cracks running along the weld. Cracks running across the weld (transverse) instead require a scan along the weld axis.
distractors: Those are found by straight-beam base-metal scans.
Scanning does not measure surface roughness.
The scan targets flaws, not couplant.

content.stem: Good practice for weld coverage is to scan:
options: From both sides of the weld and, where possible, both faces
From just one side of the weld only, in a single pass
Down the weld centerline with the beam aimed straight down
With the probe lifted clear of the surface between passes
content.explanation: Scanning from both sides and faces improves the chance of striking flaws at a favorable angle.
distractors: Single-side scanning leaves flaws undetected.
Centerline-only scanning misses the fusion faces.
The probe must remain coupled.

content.stem: Locating a reflector found with an angle beam requires combining:
options: The sound path, the refracted angle, and the surface distance
The receiver gain, the reject level, and the echo screen height
The couplant type, its film thickness, and the probe pressure
The gate width, the sweep speed, and the pulse repetition rate
content.explanation: From the sound path and angle, depth and surface distance are computed to place the reflector in the weld.
distractors: Gain does not locate a reflector.
Couplant is irrelevant to location.
Locating a reflector uses sound path and angle, not the gate width.

content.stem: Scanning gain is set above reference level so that:
options: Small or unfavorably oriented reflectors are not missed during scanning
All of the background baseline noise is wiped off the screen during scanning
The transducer crystal is held cool right through a long scanning shift
The couplant film lasts much longer between top-ups during scanning
content.explanation: Extra scanning gain raises sensitivity so marginal indications appear; evaluation then returns to reference level.
distractors: Added gain does not eliminate noise.
Gain does not cool the probe.
Gain is unrelated to couplant life.

content.stem: Adjacent scan passes should overlap by at least about:
options: Ten percent of the transducer width
Just touching with no actual overlap
Ninety percent of the transducer width
A full skip distance of the beam path
content.explanation: An overlap of roughly ten percent of the beam or probe width prevents untested gaps between passes.
distractors: Touching passes risk gaps in coverage.
Excessive overlap is inefficient and not required.
Overlap is a fraction of probe width, not a skip distance.

content.stem: Scanning speed is limited primarily by:
options: The pulse repetition rate and the operator's ability to observe indications
The thickness of the wear face fitted to the front of the contact probe
The rectification mode chosen for the signal shown on the screen display
The material that the calibration block is machined from for the setup
content.explanation: If the probe moves too fast for the pulse rate or the operator's response, small indications can pass undetected.
distractors: The wear face does not limit scan speed.
Rectification does not limit scanning speed.
Block material is unrelated to scan speed.

content.stem: Before scanning, the test surface should be:
options: Cleaned of scale, spatter, and loose debris to ensure good coupling
Left with its mill scale and loose debris kept fully in place for the scan
Coated with a fresh layer of paint to seal the surface before any scanning
Heated up to the Curie point of the material right before scanning begins
content.explanation: Removing scale, spatter, and dirt gives a clean, well-coupled surface for reliable scanning.
distractors: Debris and scale degrade coupling.
Paint can interfere with coupling and readings.
Heating to the Curie point would damage equipment.

content.stem: In immersion testing, the first large echo after the main bang is usually the:
options: Front-surface reflection from the part
The back-wall reflection from the part
An echo off the contact couplant film
A reflection from an internal flaw
content.explanation: The front-surface reflection marks where sound enters the part, ahead of any internal or back-wall echoes.
distractors: The back wall appears after the front surface.
Immersion uses a water path, not contact couplant.
A flaw echo would lie between the surfaces, not first.

content.stem: The immersion water path should be set so that:
options: The second front-surface reflection does not overlap the first back-wall echo
The water path length exactly equals the thickness of the part under test
No front-surface reflection appears at all between the part and the transducer
A thin film of grease takes the place of the water in the path to the surface
content.explanation: A water path of at least about one-quarter the part thickness keeps the second front multiple clear of the back-wall echo.
distractors: Equal path is not the criterion.
A front-surface echo always appears in immersion.
Immersion uses water, not grease.

content.stem: An interface gate (interface trigger) in immersion testing is used to:
options: Start timing from the front surface regardless of small water-path changes
Set the refracted angle the beam takes once it has entered the part below
Apply a transfer correction for the rougher surface of the actual test part
Boost the receiver gain the instant the front-surface echo arrives back
content.explanation: The interface gate references measurements to the front-surface echo, stabilizing readings as the water path varies slightly.
distractors: The gate does not change the angle.
The interface gate is not transfer correction.
It triggers timing, not gain.

content.stem: A squirter or bubbler column is used to:
options: Deliver a flowing water path for coupling without full immersion
Replace the transducer entirely with a column of fast-moving water
Generate the ultrasonic pulse directly inside the flowing water stream
Stand in for the calibration block during the entire angle-beam setup
content.explanation: Squirter and bubbler systems form a continuous water column to couple the beam in line scanning.
distractors: A transducer is still required.
It is a coupling method, not a wave generator.
It does not replace calibration.

content.stem: A wheel (rolling) transducer is advantageous because it:
options: Maintains coupling while rolling along the surface for fast scanning
Runs completely dry with no liquid sealed inside the rolling tyre at all
Is locked to one single straight-beam mode that can never be changed
Needs no calibration before it is rolled across the part
content.explanation: The liquid-filled wheel keeps a consistent coupling path while rolling, suiting production-line scanning.
distractors: It still uses liquid inside the wheel.
Wheel probes can be set for various modes.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: Compared with contact testing, immersion testing offers:
options: More consistent coupling and the option of focusing and automation
Inspection that needs no calibration references at all at any stage
Complete freedom from any temperature effect on the sound velocity
A faster result than contact testing on every kind of part without fail
content.explanation: Immersion gives uniform coupling and supports focused probes and automated scanning, useful for production work.
distractors: Immersion still needs calibration references.
Temperature still affects velocity.
It is not always faster, especially for one-off parts.

content.stem: Water used for immersion testing is usually degassed to:
options: Prevent air bubbles that cause spurious signals and coupling loss
Raise the water velocity until it matches that of the steel test part
Shift the probe frequency to a value that better suits the water path
Make the water electrically conductive enough to carry the pulse
content.explanation: Dissolved air forms bubbles on the probe and part that scatter sound and create false indications, so the water is degassed.
distractors: Degassing does not change velocity to match steel.
Degassing does not affect frequency.
Immersion does not rely on conductivity.

content.stem: Before angle-beam scanning a weld, the adjacent base metal is often checked with a straight beam to:
options: Detect laminations that could interfere with the angle-beam scan
Set the refracted angle that will be used for the angle-beam scan
Measure the outside profile and crown height of the finished weld
Fix the accept-or-reject amplitude level before the weld scan begins
content.explanation: Laminations in the scanning path can block or mislead the angle beam, so the base metal is screened first.
distractors: Base-metal scanning does not set the angle.
That is a visual or profile measurement.
Base-metal scanning screens for laminations; it does not set acceptance.

content.stem: Corrosion thickness mapping is commonly performed with:
options: A dual-element probe over a measurement grid
An angle-beam probe aimed across the welds
A surface-wave probe skimming over the plate
A through-transmission pair on either face
content.explanation: Dual-element probes read remaining wall thickness across a grid to map corrosion loss.
distractors: Angle beams are for weld flaws, not thickness mapping.
Surface waves do not measure remaining wall.
Mapping uses pulse-echo thickness readings.

content.stem: When inspecting coarse-grained material, the operator often:
options: Selects a lower frequency to reduce scatter and improve penetration
Selects a higher frequency to sharpen the resolution of the small flaws
Scans the surface fully dry with no couplant applied at any point at all
Switches the alarm gate off so that scatter cannot keep tripping the alarm
content.explanation: Lower frequencies penetrate coarse, scattering structures better, at the cost of resolution.
distractors: High frequency scatters badly in coarse grain.
Couplant is still required.
Disabling the gate does not help with scatter.

content.stem: To obtain the true amplitude of a reflector, the operator should:
options: Move the probe to maximize (peak) the echo
Take the very first echo reading shown
Turn the reject up first, then read it
Lift the probe clear off the surface
content.explanation: Peaking the echo by manipulating the probe ensures the recorded amplitude reflects the reflector's true response.
distractors: The peak, not the first reading, gives true amplitude.
Reject distorts amplitude.
That defeats the measurement.

content.stem: Distinguishing a geometric reflector (such as weld root or mismatch) from a real flaw often requires:
options: Correlating the indication's location and behavior with the weld geometry
Scanning the weld faster to see whether the indication then fades away
Switching to a much higher probe frequency and rereading the indication
Treating the indication as geometry and leaving it out of the report
content.explanation: Comparing where the indication comes from with the known weld profile helps separate harmless geometry from defects.
distractors: Speed does not distinguish geometry from a flaw.
Frequency alone does not resolve this.
Indications must be evaluated, not ignored.

content.stem: Mode-converted signals during angle-beam inspection can:
options: Produce extra indications that may be mistaken for flaws
Only ever sharpen up and clarify the true flaw indications
Never occur in steel under any incidence at the interface
Wipe out the back-wall echo for the entire rest of the scan
content.explanation: Energy converting between modes can create spurious echoes that the operator must recognize and discount.
distractors: They can confuse interpretation, not just help.
Mode conversion occurs in steel at interfaces.
They do not remove the back wall.

content.stem: A tandem technique uses two angle-beam probes to:
options: Improve detection of vertically oriented flaws in thick welds
Run the weld scan with no calibration of either probe beforehand
Launch a pair of surface waves running along the cap of the weld
Cut out the second leg of the angle-beam sound path entirely
content.explanation: In tandem, one probe transmits and another receives, favoring detection of through-thickness vertical flaws in heavy sections.
distractors: Tandem still requires calibration.
Tandem is not a surface-wave method.
Tandem does not remove a leg of the path.

content.stem: Inspecting a hot component generally requires:
options: High-temperature couplant and probes rated for the temperature
Ordinary gel couplant and any standard contact probe that is to hand
No couplant at all, since the heat itself carries the sound across
Extra receiver gain used instead of any special coupling medium
content.explanation: Heat demands special couplants and temperature-rated probes, and velocity shifts must be considered.
distractors: Ordinary couplant boils off and probes can be damaged.
Contact UT still needs coupling.
Gain does not solve the temperature problem.

content.stem: The difference between scanning level and evaluation level is that:
options: Scanning is done at a higher gain and indications are evaluated at the reference level
Scanning is done right at the reference level while indications are evaluated above it
Scanning is done at a lower gain and indications are evaluated at higher scanning gain
Both levels are set by the time of day rather than by any particular gain setting at all
content.explanation: Operators scan with extra gain to find indications, then drop to reference level to size and judge them.
distractors: Codes typically use added gain for scanning.
It is the reverse; scanning gain is higher.
Both are defined by gain settings.

content.stem: Scanning the weld root from each side using the first leg helps detect:
options: Incomplete penetration and lack of root fusion
The paint thickness left on the weld cap surface
The temperature of the couplant being applied
A mismatch in the probe cable impedance value
content.explanation: First-leg scans from both sides aim the beam at the root, where incomplete penetration and lack of fusion occur.
distractors: UT does not measure paint for this purpose.
Couplant temperature is unrelated.
Cable impedance is not a weld flaw.

content.stem: The probe angle for weld inspection is often chosen so the beam strikes the fusion face:
options: As close to perpendicular as practical
At a shallow grazing angle to the face
Running parallel along the fusion face
Aimed only at the flat back wall instead
content.explanation: Hitting the fusion face near perpendicular gives the strongest reflection from lack-of-fusion flaws there.
distractors: Grazing incidence reflects poorly back to the probe.
A parallel beam would not reflect back.
The angle targets the fusion face, not just the back wall.

content.stem: Common angle-beam refracted angles for weld inspection are:
options: 45, 60, and 70 degrees
5, 10, and 15 degrees
80, 85, and 88 degrees
30, 35, and 40 degrees
content.explanation: 45, 60, and 70 degrees are the standard shear-wave angles chosen to suit weld bevel geometry and thickness.
distractors: Those are near-straight beams, not weld angle beams.
Those approach grazing and are not standard weld angles.
Standard weld angles are 45, 60, and 70.

content.stem: A 70 degree probe compared with a 45 degree probe generally gives:
options: A longer surface distance and shallower beam path for a given depth
A much shorter surface distance and a steeper path for a given depth
A steeper and deeper beam path covering more thickness per unit travel
No change at all in the beam geometry between the two probe angles
content.explanation: Higher refracted angles spread the path out along the surface, useful for reaching flaws away from the probe.
distractors: Higher angles increase surface distance.
Higher angles travel shallower per unit surface distance.
The angle clearly changes the geometry.

content.stem: Covering a thick weld often requires:
options: Multiple probe angles and scanning from several positions
A single probe angle held at just one fixed standoff position
Straight-beam scanning aimed straight down through the weld cap
Just one leg of the beam path worked from a single side only
content.explanation: Different angles and positions reach the full bevel and thickness of a heavy weld.
distractors: One angle and position cannot cover a thick weld.
Welds need angle-beam coverage.
Both legs and several angles are needed.

content.stem: Porosity in a weld often appears on UT as:
options: Multiple small, scattered, lower-amplitude indications
A single sharp high-amplitude indication from a flat face
No reflected signal at all, since the gas pores stay silent
A taller back-wall echo than the surrounding sound metal
content.explanation: Gas pores act as many small reflectors, producing scattered low-level indications rather than one strong echo.
distractors: That is more typical of a planar flaw.
Porosity does reflect sound.
Porosity does not raise the back wall.

content.stem: Lack of fusion and incomplete penetration are well detected by angle beams because they:
options: Present flat faces favorably oriented to the angled beam
Lie flat and parallel to the scanning surface up above
Reflect only very weakly back toward the angled probe
Show up only under a straight-beam compression wave scan
content.explanation: These planar flaws lie along the fusion line, where an appropriately angled beam strikes them near perpendicular.
distractors: They are typically not parallel to the surface.
They reflect strongly when oriented to the beam.
Angle-beam shear waves detect them well.

content.stem: Scanning too quickly risks:
options: Missing small indications between pulses
Overheating the transducer crystal itself
Changing the refracted beam angle midscan
Degassing the couplant on the part surface
content.explanation: If the probe outruns the pulse rate or the operator's reaction, brief indications can be skipped.
distractors: Speed does not overheat the crystal.
Speed does not change the angle.
Speed does not degas couplant.

content.stem: An indication is generally recorded and evaluated when its amplitude:
options: Reaches or exceeds a defined reference threshold
Drops below the baseline of the display trace
Reaches the instrument's maximum gain setting
Climbs above the full back-wall echo height
content.explanation: Indications at or above the code-defined reference threshold are recorded and assessed.
distractors: Sub-baseline signals are not the recording criterion.
Recording depends on a reference threshold, not the gain ceiling.
The recording trigger is a reference threshold, not the back-wall height.

content.stem: Weld spatter left on the scanning surface can:
options: Lift the probe and break coupling, causing missed coverage
Bed the probe down and tighten its coupling onto the part
Shift the probe operating frequency up as it crosses the cap
Serve as a handy fixed reference reflector during the scan
content.explanation: Spatter creates an uneven surface that breaks contact, so it is removed before scanning.
distractors: Spatter degrades, not improves, coupling.
Spatter does not change frequency.
Spatter is debris, not a reference.

content.stem: When the weld cap cannot be removed, angle-beam scanning is preferred because it:
options: Reaches the weld volume from beside the reinforcement
Pushes a straight beam straight down through the raised cap
Forces the cap to be removed before any scan can begin
Works only once the cap is ground perfectly flush first
content.explanation: Scanning from the base metal beside the cap lets the angled beam enter the weld without removing reinforcement.
distractors: The cap blocks straight-beam access.
Angle beam avoids the need to remove the cap.
It works on an as-welded cap.

content.stem: Straight-beam thickness readings are taken from:
options: The first back-wall echo after the main bang
The third back-wall multiple in the echo train
The main bang spike at the start of the sweep
A signal sitting inside the surface dead zone
content.explanation: The time to the first back-wall echo, halved and multiplied by velocity, gives the thickness.
distractors: Thickness uses the first back wall.
The main bang is the transmit pulse, not the back wall.
The dead zone is where reading is unreliable.

content.stem: A focused immersion probe improves inspection by:
options: Concentrating energy at a chosen depth for better sensitivity there
Pressing right onto the part so that no water path is needed at all
Removing the front-surface echo from the immersion display entirely
Launching surface waves that skim across the front face of the part
content.explanation: Focusing tightens the beam at a focal depth, raising sensitivity and resolution for small reflectors there.
distractors: Immersion requires a water path.
The front-surface echo still appears.
Focusing is not about surface waves.

content.stem: Marking the half-skip and full-skip positions on the part helps the operator:
options: Know where the beam is striking through the weld thickness
Set the scanning gain to the correct level for that weld
Push every indication clear of the near-surface dead zone
Change the refracted angle partway through the scan
content.explanation: Skip references tell the operator which part of the weld the beam reaches at a given probe position.
distractors: Skip marks do not set gain.
Skip marks indicate beam position; they do not affect the dead zone.
Skip marks reference beam position; they do not change the angle.

content.stem: If an indication moves on the screen as the probe is moved but the geometry is fixed, this suggests:
options: A real reflector whose position can be tracked and located
An electronic artifact that never tracks along with the probe
Trapped couplant bubbles drifting under the probe wear face
The main bang spike held fixed at the start of the sweep
content.explanation: A reflector that moves predictably with probe position is a locatable feature to be evaluated, not noise.
distractors: An artifact would not track with probe movement consistently.
Bubbles do not track like a located reflector.
The main bang stays at the sweep start.

content.stem: Maintaining steady couplant and constant probe pressure during scanning is important because:
options: Coupling variations change signal amplitude and can mask indications
Probe pressure swings the refracted angle widely across the part
Steady pressure is what sets the sweep range across the entire screen
Constant pressure degasses the couplant film held under the probe
content.explanation: Inconsistent coupling makes amplitudes unreliable, so steady contact is needed for valid scanning.
distractors: Pressure does not change the refracted angle meaningfully.
Steady coupling keeps amplitude consistent; it does not calibrate range.
Pressure does not degas water.

content.stem: A lamination is best described as:
options: A planar separation in the base metal lying parallel to the surface
A sharp crack running straight across the thickness of the plate
A cluster of rounded gas pores trapped down within the weld bead metal
A pocket of trapped slag sitting deep inside the weld volume
content.explanation: Laminations are flat, base-metal separations parallel to the rolling surface, found with straight-beam testing.
distractors: That is a transverse crack, not a lamination.
That is porosity.
Slag is volumetric; a lamination is planar.

content.stem: Porosity typically produces:
options: Many small, scattered, lower-amplitude indications
A single sharp, high-amplitude planar indication
A complete loss of the front-surface echo from the part
No reflected sound at all back from the gas pores
content.explanation: Gas pores act as numerous small reflectors, giving a scattered, low-level response.
distractors: That is more typical of a planar flaw.
Porosity does not remove the front surface.
Porosity does reflect sound.

content.stem: Slag inclusions are generally:
options: Irregular volumetric reflectors with variable amplitude
Flat, planar reflectors that give a steady amplitude
Volumetric reflectors all aligned in one fixed direction
Reflectors too weak to detect from any probe angle
content.explanation: Trapped slag forms irregular volumetric pockets that reflect sound from many directions with varying strength.
distractors: Slag is irregular and volumetric, not flat.
Slag orientation is irregular.
Slag is detectable.

content.stem: Lack of fusion is a planar flaw located:
options: Along the weld fusion face between weld metal and base metal
Through the middle of the base-metal plate well beside the weld
Along the outer surface of the finished weld cap crown
Within the couplant film between the probe and the part
content.explanation: Lack of fusion is an unbonded planar interface at the fusion face, well detected by a beam striking it near perpendicular.
distractors: Lack of fusion is at the fusion boundary, not mid-plate.
It lies along the internal fusion line.
It is a weld flaw, not a couplant feature.

content.stem: Incomplete (lack of) penetration occurs:
options: At the weld root where the joint is not fully filled
At the weld cap where the crown is left badly overfilled
On the outer surface partway along the weld toe
In the base metal a fair distance from the joint
content.explanation: Incomplete penetration leaves the root region unfused, detectable with first-leg root scans from each side.
distractors: Incomplete penetration is a root condition.
It is located at the root of the joint.
It is a fusion-weld root flaw.

content.stem: Cracks are considered the most serious flaws because they are:
options: Planar, sharp, and able to propagate under stress
Rounded, blunt, and quite harmless under load
Always lying flat and parallel to the part surface
Too small ever to detect from any probe angle
content.explanation: A crack is a sharp planar discontinuity that concentrates stress and can grow, making it the most critical flaw.
distractors: Cracks are planar and dangerous, not harmless.
Cracks take many orientations.
Cracks are detectable, often with high amplitude when oriented.

content.stem: The key distinction between a planar and a volumetric flaw is that a planar flaw:
options: Has a flat face whose echo depends strongly on orientation
Has many curved facets that reflect sound from every direction
Is always larger in size than any volumetric flaw nearby
Cannot be detected no matter how the probe is angled
content.explanation: Planar flaws (cracks, lack of fusion) are orientation-sensitive, while volumetric flaws (porosity, slag) reflect from many angles.
distractors: That describes a volumetric flaw.
Size is not what defines planar versus volumetric.
Planar flaws are detectable when favorably oriented.

content.stem: Undercut is a discontinuity located:
options: At the weld toe on the surface, reducing the base metal section
Deep inside the weld bead, well below the visible surface
At the weld root, where the joint is left only partially filled in
In the couplant film smeared along the test surface
content.explanation: Undercut is a surface groove at the weld toe that thins the adjacent base metal.
distractors: Undercut is a surface toe condition.
Undercut is a weld surface flaw.
It is a surface weld flaw, not couplant.

content.stem: The amplitude returned from a planar flaw is highest when the flaw is:
options: Oriented perpendicular to the beam
Lying flat parallel to the beam path
Tilted at a grazing angle to it
Turned well away from the beam axis
content.explanation: A planar reflector facing the beam reflects energy straight back, giving the strongest signal.
distractors: A parallel planar flaw reflects little back to the probe.
Grazing orientation reduces the return.
Planar flaws are strongly orientation dependent.

content.stem: An unfavorably oriented crack may be missed because it:
options: Reflects sound away from the probe, returning little energy
Soaks the sound up completely so that nothing returns at all
Lifts the back-wall echo above the surrounding sound metal
Reflects only at a single fixed probe frequency setting
content.explanation: A crack angled away from the beam sends its reflection elsewhere, which is why multiple angles and scan directions are used.
distractors: Cracks reflect rather than fully absorb.
An off-angle crack does not raise the back wall.
It can still be detected from a better angle; orientation, not frequency, is the issue.

content.stem: Volumetric flaws such as porosity are less orientation-sensitive because they:
options: Reflect sound from many directions
Lie flat, locked to a single angle
Send no sound back at all to the probe
Reflect off a single flat facet only
content.explanation: Their rounded, multi-faceted surfaces scatter sound in many directions, so detection depends less on a single orientation.
distractors: They are not planar and not orientation locked.
They do reflect sound.
They reflect bulk waves from many facets.

content.stem: Using more than one probe angle on a weld improves the chance of detecting flaws because:
options: Different angles strike differently oriented flaws more favorably
More angles raise the echo amplitude from every flaw by the same amount
Several angles let the operator skip the calibration of each probe
Extra angles stop mode conversion from happening at any interface
content.explanation: A flaw missed at one angle may reflect strongly at another, so several angles increase detection probability.
distractors: Amplitude depends on flaw orientation, not just angle.
Multiple angles still require calibration.
Multiple angles do not stop mode conversion.

content.stem: In the 6 dB drop method, a flaw edge is marked where the echo:
options: Falls to half (6 dB below) its maximum amplitude
Climbs to its full peak maximum amplitude
Drops the entire way down to zero amplitude
Rises a full 6 dB above its original starting amplitude
content.explanation: When the beam is half on the flaw, the echo is 6 dB down; those probe positions mark the flaw extent.
distractors: The edge is at the drop, not the peak.
The 6 dB point is half amplitude, not zero.
The method tracks a drop, not a rise.

content.stem: The 6 dB drop method is most appropriate for flaws that are:
options: Larger than the beam width
Smaller than the beam width
Near one wavelength across
Only rounded gas pores
content.explanation: The method assumes the flaw is wide enough that moving off it halves the echo, which holds when the flaw exceeds the beam width.
distractors: Amplitude methods are unreliable for sub-beam flaws.
Size relative to the beam, not wavelength, governs the method.
It applies to extended reflectors, not only volumetric ones.

content.stem: The 20 dB drop method differs from the 6 dB method in that it:
options: Uses the beam edges defined at 20 dB down to estimate size
Marks the beam edges right at the full peak amplitude instead
Works only on scattered porosity and never on cracks
Reads the size from one single fixed probe position
content.explanation: The 20 dB drop uses the wider beam boundary at minus 20 dB, accounting for beam spread when sizing.
distractors: Edges are at the 20 dB drop, not full amplitude.
It is a general sizing method, not porosity specific.
It requires moving the probe like the 6 dB method.

content.stem: The maximum amplitude technique sizes a flaw by:
options: Tracking the peak echo as the probe moves across a multifaceted reflector
Taking just a single echo reading with the probe held perfectly still over the flaw
Counting the back-wall multiples that line up behind the flaw echo
Reading the height shown in the gate at a single fixed probe spot
content.explanation: By following successive amplitude maxima from facets of an irregular flaw, its extent can be estimated.
distractors: The method follows the moving peak, not one reading.
Multiples are not the basis of this method.
The method tracks the moving peak across the reflector, not one gate reading.

content.stem: Estimating reflector size by amplitude comparison relies on:
options: Comparing the flaw echo to a reference reflector or DAC curve
Comparing the flaw echo against the set width of the alarm gate
Comparing how fast the probe was moving across the flaw
Comparing the brightness of the signal trace on the display
content.explanation: Amplitude-based sizing compares the flaw's echo against a known reflector or the DAC to infer an equivalent size.
distractors: Sizing compares the echo to a reference, not the gate width.
Speed does not set the size estimate; the reference comparison does.
Brightness is a display setting, unrelated to sizing.

content.stem: The DGS (AVG) method estimates flaw size by:
options: Comparing the flaw echo to curves giving an equivalent flat-bottom-hole size at distance
Counting the total number of separate echoes the flaw returns across the entire sweep line
Measuring how far the flaw sits within the near-surface dead zone of the probe
Reading the refracted angle off the scale and converting that straight into a size
content.explanation: Distance Gain Size relates echo amplitude and sound path to an equivalent reflector size using standardized curves.
distractors: DGS uses amplitude and distance, not counts.
DGS is not a dead-zone measurement.
DGS does not use the angle to size.

content.stem: A limitation of amplitude-based sizing methods is that they:
options: Estimate length better than through-wall height
Estimate through-wall height better than length
Are never used to size length on extended flaws
Need no reference reflector or DAC curve at all
content.explanation: Amplitude sizing works reasonably for length but poorly for through-wall extent, where tip-based methods are preferred.
distractors: Amplitude methods are weak at through-wall height.
They are commonly used for length.
They rely on a reference or curve.

content.stem: Tip-diffraction sizing estimates a crack's height by:
options: Detecting signals diffracted from the crack tips
Detecting only the corner echo from the crack base
Counting the back-wall multiples seen behind it
Reading only the peak amplitude of the crack echo
content.explanation: Weak diffracted signals from the upper and lower crack tips locate them, giving through-wall height more accurately than amplitude.
distractors: Tip diffraction uses tip signals, not just the corner.
Back-wall counts do not give crack height.
Tip diffraction uses tip signals, not peak amplitude alone.

content.stem: Length sizing of an extended flaw is done by:
options: Moving the probe along the flaw and marking where the response meets the drop criterion
Holding the probe at a single fixed position and reading the length straight off the screen
Raising the probe frequency until the entire length of the flaw appears on the display
Measuring the width of the main bang spike over at the far left of the sweep line
content.explanation: Traversing the flaw and noting the edge positions by the chosen drop criterion establishes its length.
distractors: A single position cannot measure length.
Frequency change does not size length.
The main bang does not indicate flaw length.

content.stem: Amplitude sizing of a flaw smaller than the beam tends to:
options: Be unreliable, since the echo never reaches a full-beam response
Be highly reliable, since the small flaw still fills the entire beam
Carry only a tiny error, well within the usual tolerance band
Need no reference reflector at all to give a sound result
content.explanation: When the flaw is smaller than the beam, the beam is never fully on it, so amplitude does not map cleanly to size.
distractors: Sub-beam flaws give unreliable amplitude sizing.
The error is significant, not slight.
A reference is still needed and still imperfect.

content.stem: Comparing a flaw echo to a side-drilled hole reference allows the operator to express size as:
options: An amplitude relative to the reference, such as a percentage of DAC or dB above or below
An exact crack height in millimeters read directly straight off the screen position itself
An exact volumetric size in cubic millimeters for the entire flaw body
A plain pass or fail result, with no amplitude figure recorded at all
content.explanation: Indications are reported relative to the reference, for example as percent DAC or decibels above or below reference.
distractors: Reference comparison gives relative amplitude, not exact height.
The comparison gives a relative amplitude, not an exact volume.
The result is expressed as amplitude relative to the reference.

content.stem: A reduction in back-wall echo together with no clear flaw echo can indicate:
options: A flaw scattering or absorbing sound, or high attenuation
A perfectly sound part with no flaw present anywhere
A rise in the back-wall echo well above the normal level
A couplant problem only, and never an actual flaw in the part
content.explanation: Even without a distinct flaw echo, a dropped back wall warns of scattering, absorption, or an unfavorably oriented flaw.
distractors: Loss of back wall suggests something is interfering.
Loss of back wall is a drop, not an increase.
Loss of back wall can mean a flaw, not just couplant.

content.stem: The recording level is the amplitude at which an indication is:
options: Documented for further evaluation
Rejected straight away as a flaw
Erased from the inspection record
Ignored and left fully unrecorded
content.explanation: Indications reaching the recording level are written down so they can be evaluated against acceptance criteria.
distractors: Recording is not the same as rejection.
Recording means documenting, not erasing.
Recording means it is noted, not ignored.

content.stem: The evaluation level is where an indication is:
options: Assessed in detail to determine its significance
Discarded without any further review being done
Erased from the screen before it can be read
Coupled to the surface with extra gel beforehand
content.explanation: At the evaluation level the operator characterizes and measures the indication to judge acceptability.
distractors: Evaluation means review, not discarding.
At the evaluation level the indication is assessed, not erased.
Evaluation is unrelated to couplant.

content.stem: The acceptance or rejection level for an indication is set by:
options: The governing code or specification
The operator's own personal preference
The instrument maker's own choice
The couplant supplier's own advice
content.explanation: Acceptance and rejection thresholds are defined by the applicable code or specification, not chosen arbitrarily.
distractors: Accept or reject criteria come from the code, not preference.
The code, not the maker, sets acceptance.
Couplant suppliers do not set acceptance levels.

content.stem: A relevant indication is one that:
options: Is caused by an actual discontinuity requiring evaluation
Comes from the part geometry such as a counterbore or root
Comes from electrical noise with no real reflector behind it
Must always be rejected the very moment it is recorded
content.explanation: Relevant indications arise from real discontinuities and must be evaluated, though not all are rejectable.
distractors: That is a non-relevant geometric indication.
That is a false indication.
Relevant does not automatically mean rejectable.

content.stem: A non-relevant indication typically arises from:
options: Part geometry such as a counterbore, root, or change in section
A crack lying along the fusion face of the actual welded joint
Electrical noise with no real reflector sitting behind it at all
A flat lamination running through the base-metal plate body
content.explanation: Non-relevant indications come from geometric features rather than defects, and must be recognized as such.
distractors: A crack is a relevant flaw indication.
That would be a false indication.
A lamination is a relevant flaw.

content.stem: A false indication is one that:
options: Does not correspond to a real reflector, such as electrical noise or interference
Comes from a sharp crack lying right along the fusion face of the actual welded joint
Comes from the part geometry, such as a counterbore or a change of section
Comes from a real measured flaw that has been sized against the reference curve
content.explanation: False indications are artifacts such as electrical noise or interference, with no real reflector behind them. (Mode-converted echoes are different: they come from real sound paths and geometry, so they are spurious rather than truly false.)
distractors: A crack gives a relevant, not false, indication.
That is a non-relevant geometric indication.
False indications are artifacts, not measured flaws.

content.stem: Distinguishing a geometric root indication from a root flaw often requires:
options: Correlating the indication position with the known weld geometry
Turning the receiver gain up until the root signal stands well clear
Changing the couplant to a thicker gel before reading the root again
Switching the alarm gate off so that the root echo can be read
content.explanation: Knowing where the beam strikes relative to the weld profile helps separate harmless geometry from genuine root flaws.
distractors: More gain alone does not separate geometry from a flaw.
Couplant change does not resolve this.
The gate is used, not removed.

content.stem: Evaluating an indication fully means determining its:
options: Location, amplitude, length, and likely type
The echo amplitude alone and nothing else
Location and length, but never its amplitude
The impedance of the probe cable being used
content.explanation: A complete evaluation records where the flaw is, how strong it is, how long it is, and what kind it appears to be.
distractors: Amplitude by itself does not characterize a flaw.
A full evaluation needs location, amplitude, length, and type.
Cable impedance is unrelated.

content.stem: Echo amplitude alone is an unreliable indicator of flaw size because it also depends on:
options: Flaw orientation, shape, and distance
The name of the operator on the shift
The brightness setting on the display
The temperature of the work area alone
content.explanation: Two flaws of equal size can give very different echoes depending on orientation, surface, and range, so amplitude is not size.
distractors: The operator's name does not affect echo amplitude.
Brightness is a display setting, not a factor in true amplitude.
Temperature is minor here; orientation, shape, and distance dominate.

content.stem: The depth of a flaw found with an angle beam is calculated from:
options: The sound path and the refracted angle
The receiver gain and the reject level
The couplant type and its film thickness
The trace brightness and the sweep speed
content.explanation: Depth equals sound path times the cosine of the refracted angle (corrected for the leg), placing the flaw through the thickness.
distractors: Gain does not give depth.
Couplant does not locate the flaw.
Depth comes from sound path and angle, not brightness.

content.stem: The surface distance from the index point to a flaw is calculated from:
options: The sound path and the sine of the refracted angle
The reject level set with the receiver gain
The count of the back-wall multiples on the screen
The display rectification mode currently in use
content.explanation: Surface distance equals sound path times the sine of the refracted angle, giving where the flaw lies along the surface.
distractors: Reject does not locate the flaw.
Multiples are not used for surface distance.
Surface distance uses sound path and angle, not the display mode.

content.stem: Determining whether a flaw is on the first or second leg is important because it:
options: Changes how depth is calculated from the sound path
Sets how fast the probe is moved across the weld
Decides which couplant gel gets used on the part
Makes no real difference to the final depth calculation
content.explanation: On the second leg, depth is found from 2T minus the raw reading, so identifying the leg is essential to locate the flaw correctly.
distractors: The leg affects how depth is computed, not scan speed.
The leg does not select couplant.
The leg significantly affects the depth calculation.

content.stem: Plotting a flaw on a weld cross-section helps the operator:
options: Show where the flaw lies relative to the weld and judge its significance
Set the correct scanning gain to use just before the weld is examined again
Calibrate the horizontal sweep range right across the entire screen
Change the refracted angle that the beam takes inside the part
content.explanation: A scale plot places the flaw within the weld profile, aiding evaluation against acceptance criteria.
distractors: Plotting records position; it does not set gain.
Plotting locates the flaw; it does not calibrate range.
Plotting records position, it does not change the angle.

content.stem: The orientation of a planar flaw can be inferred by:
options: Comparing its response from different angles and scan directions
Taking one single reading with the probe held perfectly still on the flaw
Watching how the couplant spreads out under the moving probe
Counting the back-wall multiples that sit behind the flaw echo
content.explanation: A flaw that responds strongly at one angle and weakly at another reveals the direction its face is pointing.
distractors: One reading does not reveal orientation.
Couplant does not indicate orientation.
Back-wall counts do not give orientation.

content.stem: Two closely spaced reflectors may be displayed as one indication if:
options: The instrument resolution is insufficient to separate them
The receiver gain is set far too low to show both echoes
The couplant film under the probe is just a little too thick
The probe cable is too long for the two echoes to separate
content.explanation: Limited resolution merges close reflectors, so a single indication may actually be more than one flaw.
distractors: Low gain hides signals but is not the resolution issue.
Couplant thickness is not the separation factor.
Cable length does not merge reflectors.

content.stem: A cluster of small scattered indications that rises and falls as the probe moves most likely represents:
options: Scattered porosity rather than a single planar flaw
A single tight crack running along the fusion face
A broad flat lamination lying in the base metal
Pure electrical noise with no real reflector at all
content.explanation: Many small, varying indications across a region are characteristic of distributed porosity.
distractors: A crack gives a more coherent, oriented response.
A lamination is a broad parallel reflector, not scattered.
The behavior tracks real reflectors, not noise.

content.stem: A long, coherent, high-amplitude planar indication along the fusion line most likely indicates:
options: Lack of fusion or a crack
A scattered band of weld porosity
Weld toe undercut
A couplant air gap
content.explanation: A strong, continuous planar response along the fusion face points to lack of fusion or a crack there.
distractors: Porosity is scattered, not a coherent planar line.
Undercut is a surface toe feature.
A couplant gap is not a fusion-line flaw.

content.stem: To detect a transverse crack (one running across the weld), the probe is oriented to send its beam along the weld axis because such cracks:
options: Face along the weld axis, so a beam aimed across the weld reflects poorly off them
Lie flat and parallel to the surface, much like a flat lamination in the base metal
Cannot be detected by ultrasound from any scan direction
Show up only under a straight-beam compression wave aimed from above
content.explanation: A transverse crack runs across the weld, so its face is roughly perpendicular to the weld axis. A beam directed along the weld axis strikes that face near-perpendicular and reflects strongly, while the usual across-weld beam glances off it. The probe is placed to shoot parallel to the weld and moved along it for coverage.
distractors: Transverse cracks are not surface-parallel laminations.
They can be detected with the right scan direction.
Angle-beam axial scanning detects them.

content.stem: When sizing with the 6 dB drop method, the reference maximum is taken as:
options: The peak echo with the beam fully on the flaw
The echo seen right at the very edge of the flaw
The back-wall echo seen behind the flaw
The first echo seen well before the peak
content.explanation: The flaw's maximum echo with the beam centered on it is the reference from which the 6 dB drop edges are found.
distractors: The reference is the full-on peak, not the edge.
The back wall is not the sizing reference here.
The method requires the true peak as reference.

content.stem: An indication that stays fixed on the screen while the probe moves is most likely:
options: An instrument artifact or electrical signal rather than a reflector in the part
A real reflector inside the part that the operator can track and then locate
A geometric indication from the weld root that moves with the probe position
A flat lamination in the base metal that responds clearly as the probe is being moved
content.explanation: A real reflector changes sound path as the probe moves; a signal that does not move is likely an artifact.
distractors: A real reflector moves with probe position.
Geometry indications still track with probe position.
A lamination would respond to probe movement.

content.stem: The corner (90 degree) reflection that makes surface-breaking cracks detectable arises from:
options: Sound reflecting off the crack face and the adjoining surface back to the probe
Sound being soaked up by the crack face so that little returns to the probe
The crack resonating at the probe frequency and then re-radiating all that energy back
The couplant pooling in the crack mouth and bouncing the sound straight back
content.explanation: The right-angle between a surface-breaking crack and the surface acts as a corner reflector, returning a strong echo.
distractors: The corner effect reflects energy, not absorbs it.
The corner effect is a geometric reflection from the right angle, not resonance.
The corner reflection is geometric, not couplant.

content.stem: If two amplitude sizing methods give different lengths for the same flaw, the operator should:
options: Follow the method specified by the governing code or procedure
Average the two lengths together and record the middle figure
Choose the smaller length so that the flaw passes acceptance
Leave the flaw unsized and simply note both readings on the report
content.explanation: The applicable procedure dictates which sizing method and criteria apply, ensuring consistent, defensible results.
distractors: The code, not an arbitrary average, governs.
Choosing to pass a flaw is improper.
The flaw must be sized per procedure.

content.stem: Comparing an indication's amplitude to the DAC curve at the same distance tells the operator:
options: How the indication's response compares to the reference reflector at that depth
Exactly what type of flaw is present, be it a crack, slag, or porosity
The precise orientation of the flaw face relative to the angled incident sound beam
The remaining wall thickness left beneath the indication at that point
content.explanation: Reading the indication against the DAC at its distance shows whether it is above or below the reference response there.
distractors: Amplitude comparison does not give the flaw type.
DAC comparison gives relative amplitude, not orientation.
DAC comparison is about amplitude versus the reference, not wall thickness.

content.stem: Before rejecting an indication, the operator should confirm it is:
options: A relevant indication from a real discontinuity, not geometry or an artifact
An indication that has simply been written down somewhere on the report
An indication that peaks once the gain is run up to its full maximum
An indication that happens to lie close to the probe on the part surface only
content.explanation: Rejection follows confirming the indication is real and relevant and that it exceeds the code's acceptance criteria.
distractors: Being recorded is not enough to reject.
Maximum gain is not a rejection basis.
Proximity to the probe is not a rejection basis.

content.stem: Comparing the flaw response at 45 and 60 degrees can help because a flaw that:
options: Responds much more strongly at one angle suggests a specific orientation
Responds equally at both angles is proof the flaw must be a crack
Gives no response at either angle is fair grounds enough to reject it outright
Shifts the probe frequency each time the refracted angle is changed
content.explanation: A large difference in response between angles reveals the flaw's facing direction, aiding characterization.
distractors: Equal response does not prove a crack.
No response is not a basis for rejection.
Angle does not change the probe frequency.

content.stem: The inspection record for an evaluated indication should include:
options: Its location, amplitude, length, and characterization
Only the operator's name signed at the foot of the report sheet
Just its amplitude by itself, with nothing more
Only the date that the inspection was carried out
content.explanation: A complete report documents where the flaw is, its amplitude and length, and what it appears to be, for disposition.
distractors: A full record needs the indication data, not just a name.
A complete record needs location, amplitude, length, and characterization.
Date alone does not document the indication.

content.stem: API 1104 covers the welding of:
options: Pipelines and related facilities
Boilers and pressure vessels
Structural building steelwork
Aircraft and spacecraft frames
content.explanation: API 1104 is the standard for welding pipelines and related facilities carrying oil, gas, and related products.
distractors: Those fall under ASME, not API 1104.
That is covered by AWS D1.1.
Aerospace welding is outside API 1104.

content.stem: Under API 1104, a defect is:
options: An imperfection of sufficient magnitude to warrant rejection
Any imperfection at all, no matter how small its size or type
A geometric profile feature left behind by the weld root pass
A normal sound feature of any fully acceptable weld
content.explanation: The code distinguishes an imperfection (any discontinuity) from a defect, which is an imperfection large enough to be rejectable.
distractors: Not every imperfection is a defect; only those exceeding criteria.
Geometry is not a defect.
A sound weld feature is not a defect.

content.stem: Under API 1104, the acceptance criteria for a discontinuity are established by:
options: The governing code, applied per the method and criteria it specifies
The inspector's personal preference, set fresh for each weld examined
The pipe manufacturer's own in-house standard for that pipe grade
The welding crew's agreed view on the day the job is run
content.explanation: Acceptance criteria are defined by the governing code and applied using the method and limits it specifies, not chosen by the operator, manufacturer, or crew.
distractors: Acceptance comes from the code, not operator preference.
The code, not the pipe maker, sets acceptance.
The crew does not set acceptance criteria.

content.stem: API 1104 provides two routes to acceptance: the standard workmanship criteria and:
options: Alternative acceptance criteria based on fracture mechanics and fitness for service
A route that simply ignores any imperfection found below the weld cap surface
Acceptance left entirely to the personal judgment of the welder making the joint
A route that drops all NDE entirely once the procedure has been qualified
content.explanation: Besides workmanship-based limits, the code allows an alternative (engineering critical assessment) route using fracture mechanics and known flaw sizes.
distractors: No route ignores imperfections.
Acceptance is not left to welder judgment.
NDE is still required.

content.stem: A distinguishing feature of API 1104 acceptance criteria compared with amplitude-based codes is that they rely heavily on:
options: Imperfection type and dimension such as length
Echo amplitude read directly off the screen
The scanning gain chosen for the inspection
The couplant chosen during the scan pass
content.explanation: API 1104 judges many imperfections by their type and length rather than primarily by amplitude relative to a reference reflector. Amplitude still plays a role in evaluation, but disposition is largely length and type driven.
distractors: API 1104 leans on type and size, not amplitude alone.
Acceptance leans on type and length, not the scanning gain.
Couplant is not an acceptance criterion.

content.stem: The alternative acceptance criteria in API 1104 generally require:
options: Stress analysis and reliable flaw sizing to assess fitness for service
A simple visual check of the cap alone to judge fitness for service
A drop in scanning sensitivity so more of the borderline flaws pass
No need to know the pipe wall thickness at all during the assessment
content.explanation: Fitness-for-service acceptance depends on stress levels, material toughness, and accurate flaw dimensions, so reliable sizing is essential.
distractors: The alternative route needs analysis and sizing, not just visual.
It does not reduce sensitivity.
Wall thickness is central to the assessment.

content.stem: In API 1104 work, ultrasonic testing is commonly used as:
options: An alternative or supplement to radiography for girth weld inspection
A way to qualify the welders so that they need no separate test
A check of the base metal only, leaving the weld itself unexamined
A replacement for the code itself once all the welds are made
content.explanation: UT, including mechanized systems, is widely accepted under API 1104 for inspecting pipeline girth welds.
distractors: UT does not replace qualifying welders.
UT inspects the weld, not only base metal.
UT is a method applied under the code, not a substitute for it.

content.stem: Automated ultrasonic testing (AUT) of mechanized girth welds typically uses:
options: Zonal discrimination, dividing the weld bevel into zones each monitored by a focused probe
A single broad channel watching the whole weld bevel at once from one fixed probe
A radiographic film exposure taken right around the full girth of the weld
A manual operator sweeping a hand probe along every girth weld in turn
content.explanation: Zonal discrimination assigns a focused transducer to each vertical zone of the bevel, matching the weld passes for fast, repeatable coverage.
distractors: AUT uses multiple zoned, focused channels.
AUT is ultrasonic, not radiographic.
AUT is mechanized, not manual.

content.stem: A practical advantage of AUT with zonal discrimination on pipeline girth welds is:
options: Fast, consistent, real-time coverage suited to mechanized production welding
Complete coverage with no calibration needed at all before the run begins
Inspection carried out without any transducers along the scanning ring
Coverage that needs no qualified operators at all once it is set up
content.explanation: AUT keeps pace with mechanized welding, giving immediate, repeatable results across the weld zones.
distractors: AUT still requires calibration.
Transducers are central to AUT.
Qualified operators are still required.

content.stem: In AUT zonal discrimination, each zone's focused probe is set to:
options: Interrogate a specific depth and region of the weld bevel
Cover the entire weld bevel from root to cap all at once
Screen the surrounding base metal for laminations only first
Replace the back-wall echo used during the thickness check
content.explanation: Each channel is focused on its assigned zone so that an indication can be tied to a particular part of the weld cross-section.
distractors: Each probe targets its own zone, not the whole weld.
Each zone interrogates its assigned region of the bevel, not base-metal screening.
The zonal probes do not replace the back wall.

content.stem: Manual ultrasonic testing under API 1104 is:
options: Permitted when performed to a qualified procedure by qualified personnel
Never allowed under any circumstance at all once AUT is available
Allowed freely with no written procedure needed at all beforehand
Limited to checking the base metal and never the weld itself
content.explanation: Manual UT is acceptable provided it follows a qualified procedure and is done by qualified technicians.
distractors: Manual UT is allowed under qualified conditions.
A qualified procedure is required.
Manual UT inspects welds under the code.

content.stem: Under API 1104, NDT personnel performing UT must be:
options: Qualified in accordance with a recognized written practice or program
Approved directly by the pipe manufacturer for that one grade of pipe
Allowed to work unqualified so long as a qualified hand supervises them
Free to work with no formal qualification of any kind whatsoever
content.explanation: The code requires UT personnel to be qualified under a recognized program such as a written practice referencing ASNT guidelines.
distractors: Qualification follows a written practice, not the pipe maker.
Even supervised work requires qualified personnel for evaluation.
Qualification is required.

content.stem: Before production welding under API 1104, the welding procedure must be:
options: Qualified to demonstrate it can produce sound welds
Qualified only once the first joints have been welded
Accepted on the welder's experience with no test at all
Qualified only after a weld has failed in service first
content.explanation: A qualified welding procedure specification must be established before production to show the process yields acceptable welds.
distractors: Qualification precedes production welding.
Experience does not replace procedure qualification.
Qualification is done up front, not after a failure.

content.stem: Welder qualification under API 1104 establishes that:
options: The welder can produce welds meeting the code using the qualified procedure
The welder may work to any personal method outside the qualified procedure
The welder's joints need no further inspection at all once qualified
The welder may pick any filler metal at all regardless of the procedure
content.explanation: Welder qualification demonstrates the individual can make acceptable welds under the qualified procedure.
distractors: Welders must follow the qualified procedure.
Welder qualification does not remove inspection.
Filler metal is an essential variable, not a free choice.

content.stem: A change in an essential variable of a qualified welding procedure generally requires:
options: Requalification of the procedure
Just a quick note in the file
A brief note added in the log
A sign-off by the site inspector
content.explanation: Essential variables are those whose change affects weld properties, so altering one requires the procedure to be requalified.
distractors: Changing an essential variable triggers requalification.
A change needs formal requalification, not just a note.
The inspector is unrelated to procedure variables.

content.stem: Inadequate penetration in a pipeline girth weld refers to:
options: Weld metal failing to extend through and fill the root
Weld metal piled up well above the cap surface of the joint
A groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe
Rounded gas voids trapped through the weld body metal
content.explanation: Inadequate penetration is a root condition where the weld metal does not extend through and fill the joint root. It is distinct from incomplete fusion, which is a lack of bond rather than a lack of fill.
distractors: That is overfill, not inadequate penetration.
That is undercut.
That is porosity.

content.stem: Incomplete fusion is:
options: A lack of bonding between weld metal and base metal or between passes
A scatter of rounded gas voids trapped within the weld bead body
Molten metal blown clean through the root and into the pipe bore
A thin oxide film left across the finished surface of the cap
content.explanation: Incomplete fusion is a planar lack of bond at the fusion face or between passes, well suited to angle-beam detection.
distractors: That is porosity.
That is burn-through or overfill.
Incomplete fusion is an unbonded interface, not just oxide.

content.stem: Internal concavity in a girth weld is:
options: A root condition where the fused weld surface lies below the pipe inner surface
A sharp crack opening at the cap on the outer surface of the finished weld
A pocket of trapped slag sitting low within the main body of the weld
A patch of undercut melted into the toe right along the weld
content.explanation: Internal concavity describes a fused but recessed root surface; the code treats it as its own imperfection category.
distractors: Internal concavity is a root profile, not a cap crack.
It is a profile condition, not slag.
That is a different surface condition.

content.stem: Burn-through is best described as:
options: Excessive penetration where molten metal is blown into the pipe bore
Too little penetration, leaving the root short of being fully filled
A small scar struck onto the surface by a stray welding arc tip
A flat separation lying within the pipe base-metal wall itself
content.explanation: Burn-through results from excessive heat collapsing the molten root into the bore, a distinct rejectable condition.
distractors: That is inadequate penetration, the opposite.
An arc strike is a different surface condition.
Burn-through is a weld condition, not a lamination.

content.stem: Elongated slag inclusions are:
options: Linear nonmetallic material trapped in the weld
Rounded gas voids scattered through the bead
Unbonded faces lying between adjacent weld passes
A groove melted along the toe of the weld
content.explanation: Slag inclusions are trapped nonmetallic residue; elongated ones run lengthwise and are a defined imperfection type.
distractors: Those are porosity, not slag.
Those are lack of fusion.
Undercut is a surface toe groove.

content.stem: Porosity in a weld is:
options: Gas entrapment forming rounded voids
A sharp planar crack through the weld
An unbonded face between the passes
Trapped solid nonmetallic matter
content.explanation: Porosity is gas trapped during solidification, appearing as rounded voids the code addresses separately from cluster porosity.
distractors: Cracks are planar, not rounded voids.
That is incomplete fusion.
Slag is nonmetallic solid, not gas porosity.

content.stem: Under API 1104, cracks are generally:
options: Cause for rejection, with only very limited defined exceptions
Freely accepted so long as they stay below the cap surface line
Treated as less serious than a patch of scattered weld porosity
Acceptable whenever they sit fully buried inside the weld body
content.explanation: Cracks are planar and propagate, so the code rejects them (9.3.10); the only exception is a crater or star crack no longer than 5/32 in. (4 mm).
distractors: Cracks are generally rejectable, not freely accepted.
Cracks are more critical than porosity.
Buried cracks are still evaluated and generally rejectable.

content.stem: Undercut in a girth weld is:
options: A groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe
Rounded gas voids trapped right through the weld bead
Molten metal blown through the root and into the bore
Linear nonmetallic matter trapped within the weld
content.explanation: Undercut is a surface groove at the toe that reduces the adjacent base metal thickness, a defined surface imperfection.
distractors: That is porosity.
That is burn-through.
That is slag.

content.stem: API 1104 addresses an accumulation of imperfections because:
options: Several small imperfections within a length of weld can together be rejectable
Only one single imperfection at a time is ever judged against the code limit
An accumulation of small flaws can never on its own be a cause for rejection
It applies to the base metal alone and never to the weld body itself
content.explanation: The code caps the combined length of imperfections within any continuous 12 in. (300 mm) of weld and against an 8 % of weld-length limit, so many small ones can together exceed acceptance.
distractors: The code considers accumulated imperfections, not just single ones.
Accumulation can be cause for rejection.
It applies to the weld, not just base metal.

content.stem: When evaluating a UT indication under API 1104, a primary measured characteristic is the indication's:
options: Length
Color
Angle
Speed
content.explanation: Indication length is a central measured parameter when applying the code's dimension-based acceptance limits.
distractors: Screen color is not an acceptance characteristic.
The measured characteristic of the indication is its length, not the beam angle.
Scan speed is not the measured indication characteristic.

content.stem: Whether an imperfection is surface-connected or buried matters under API 1104 because:
options: Acceptance limits can differ for surface and buried imperfections
Scan speed must be raised for every surface-connected imperfection
A different couplant is required for surface versus buried flaws
It makes no difference at all to the acceptance limit applied
content.explanation: The code may treat surface-breaking imperfections more conservatively than buried ones, so the distinction affects disposition.
distractors: Surface versus buried changes the applicable acceptance limit, not scan speed.
Couplant is unrelated to acceptance.
Surface versus buried can change the applicable limit.

content.stem: Determining the orientation of a weld flaw (transverse versus longitudinal) matters because it:
options: Affects how the flaw is detected and which scanning is needed
Sets the diameter of pipe that the procedure may be used on
Fixes the welding current that is used to make the girth weld
Has no real effect at all on detection or the scanning chosen
content.explanation: A transverse flaw requires scanning along the weld, while a longitudinal one is found scanning across it, so orientation drives the approach.
distractors: Orientation does not change the pipe size.
Orientation is unrelated to welding current.
Orientation strongly affects detection and scanning.

content.stem: A non-relevant indication from weld root geometry under API 1104 should be:
options: Recognized as geometric and not recorded as a defect
Recorded straight away as a rejectable weld defect itself
Treated as a root crack and removed by grinding it out
Repaired under a qualified weld repair procedure first
content.explanation: Geometric reflectors from root or counterbore are non-relevant and must be distinguished from actual imperfections.
distractors: Geometry is not automatically a defect.
Geometry is not a crack.
Non-relevant geometry does not require repair.

content.stem: Under API 1104, a weld containing a defect must generally be:
options: Repaired or removed in accordance with qualified procedures
Left in service so long as it is noted on the report sheet
Painted over to seal the defect against the weather outside
Accepted on the signature of the welder who first made it
content.explanation: Defects must be repaired by qualified repair procedures or the weld removed, not left in place.
distractors: A defect cannot simply be left in service.
Painting does not address a weld defect.
Welder approval does not accept a defect.

content.stem: Repairing a crack under API 1104 requires:
options: Complete removal of the crack before rewelding, per a qualified repair procedure
Welding straight over the crack to seal it shut without removing any of it first
Leaving the crack in place whenever it sits down below the cap of the weld
Rewelding the area with no further inspection at all once the repair is done
content.explanation: A crack must be fully excavated before any rewelding, following a qualified repair procedure, then reinspected.
distractors: A crack must be removed, not welded over.
Cracks are generally removed regardless.
Repairs are reinspected.

content.stem: After a weld repair is completed, the repaired area must be:
options: Reinspected by the applicable NDE method
Documented only, with no further checks
Given a quick visual look, then passed
Logged on the report sheet and left there
content.explanation: Repaired welds are reinspected to confirm the defect was removed and the repair is acceptable.
distractors: Repairs require reinspection.
The applicable NDE method, not visual alone, is used.
Reinspection is required, not just documentation.

content.stem: Inspection records under API 1104 should document:
options: The welds examined, the results, and the disposition of indications
Only the names of the welders who ran each joint along the line
The weather conditions that were present on the day the welds were made
Only the welds that passed, leaving the rejects right off the record
content.explanation: Documentation records what was inspected, the findings, and how indications were dispositioned, supporting traceability.
distractors: Records cover examination results, not just names.
Weather is not the inspection record.
Records are kept whether or not welds pass.

content.stem: Under API 1104, a UT procedure used for production must be:
options: Established and qualified before it is applied to production welds
Written up only after the production welds have all been examined
Accepted on the crew's experience with no formal qualification at all
Identical to the radiographic procedure used on those very joints
